summary: Togo is a long, narrow country on the Gulf of Guinea coast of West Africa; it was a German colony and was later ruled by France, becoming independent in 1960.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: In 1847 the German Bremen Mission began preaching among the Ewe, and after Germany made Togo a protectorate in 1884, the Catholic Society of the Divine Word came in 1892 and ran schools in the south. After World War I Togo was divided between Britain and France, and the Catholic and Protestant churches in French Togo continued to develop. Because mission schools were the main route to education and jobs, Christianity became especially widespread on the southern coast and in the cities.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs
ranking.description: The Vodun of the Ewe and Mina worships various spirits (vodun) and ancestors, holding that the spirits govern nature and human affairs, and there are still specialized priests and shrines today. The Akodessewa fetish market in the capital, Lomé, sells all kinds of ritual items for Vodun ceremonies, and the Kabiye in the north also keep traditional rituals such as the initiation wrestling called evala. Many Christians also take part in traditional rituals, so the share of traditional belief is high.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam arrived in the 18th–19th centuries with Muslim traders such as the Hausa and Dyula traveling south along inland trade routes, and is concentrated mainly in Sokodé in the center and Mango in the north. Most of the Tem (Kotokoli) people of the center are Muslim, while the southern coast, where Christian missions came earlier, has fewer Muslims.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Those with no religion are found mainly in cities such as Lomé and are related to urbanization and modern education. However, in Togolese society religion is closely bound up with family and ethnic identity, and most people maintain some relationship with a faith or traditional ritual, so the share of those who clearly state they have no religion is not high.

religion.background: The Ewe and Mina of southern Togo long followed Vodun, and the peoples of the north also keep their own ancestor veneration and traditional rituals. In the 18th–19th centuries Muslim traders brought Islam into the center and north. German missionaries began preaching in 1847, and after Germany founded the colony in 1884 Catholicism and Protestantism developed rapidly. After World War I Togo was divided between Britain and France, and French Togo became independent in 1960; today Christianity, traditional belief and Islam coexist and often blend with one another.

language.official: French is the official language, and Ewe and Kabiye are national languages.

ranking.name: Ewe
ranking.description: Ewe belongs to the Gbe group of the Niger–Congo family and is the language of the Ewe and Mina of the south. In the 19th century missionaries of the German Bremen Mission devised a writing system for Ewe and translated the Bible, making it one of the earliest languages in West Africa to have a written standard. Because Ewe and the closely related Mina are the common language of the south and of the Lomé market, it has the most speakers in the country, and in 1975 the government also made it a national language.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: French was introduced in the French Mandate period (1919–1960) after World War I, replacing German as the language of administration and education, and it was kept as the sole official language after independence in 1960. French is in common use in government, schools and the media, but most people have an indigenous language as their mother tongue and can use French fluently only after being educated, so its share as a main language is not high.

language.history: Togo has about 40 languages, with Ewe and Mina predominant in the south and Kabiye, Tem and others in the north. In the 19th century German missionaries established a written standard for Ewe, and during the German colonial period (1884–1914) German was also a school language. After World War I France ruled most of Togo and French became the official language. In 1975 the government made Ewe and Kabiye national languages and promoted them in school education.

ranking.name: Fufu
ranking.description: Boiled yam (or cassava) is pounded repeatedly in a wooden mortar with a long pestle into an elastic white dough, eaten with palm nut soup or peanut stew.
ranking.history: The yam has been the staple of the West African "yam belt" for thousands of years, and cassava was introduced from the Americas by the Portuguese after the 16th century; both can be made into fufu. Pounding fufu takes two people, one holding the pestle and one turning the dough, and in West Africa it is an everyday scene representing the division of labor and togetherness of the family. The Ewe and the peoples of the north each have an annual festival celebrating the yam harvest, and the capital, Lomé, has many small shops specializing in fufu.

ranking.name: Palm nut soup
ranking.description: Oil palm fruits are boiled soft and pounded, the orange-red juice is extracted, and it is simmered with fish, chicken or beef and chili into a rich soup, often served with fufu or rice.
ranking.history: The oil palm is native to West Africa and has been the main local source of fat for thousands of years. After the slave trade was banned in the 19th century, the West African coast turned to exporting palm oil to Europe for soap and machine lubricants, which was called "legitimate trade"; during the German colonial period palm planting was also promoted in Togo. Palm nut soup has therefore become the most representative soup of southern Togo, especially common at festivals and family gatherings.

ranking.name: Abloh (steamed corn cake)
ranking.description: A batter of fermented maize or rice flour is mixed with a little sugar and steamed in leaves or molds into small white, slightly sweet steamed cakes, often served with fried fish and chili sauce.
ranking.history: Maize is native to the Americas and was brought to the West African coast by the Portuguese after the 16th century, quickly becoming an important local crop. Abloh is a traditional snack of the Ewe and Mina along the coasts of Togo and Benin, and fermentation gives the cakes a slightly sour flavor and lets them keep a little longer. On the streets of Lomé abloh is often sold together with fried fish and chili-tomato sauce and is a representative snack of the coastal region.

ranking.name: Gboma dessi (garden egg leaf stew)
ranking.description: A vegetable stew of the tender leaves of the African eggplant (called "gboma" locally) stewed with tomato, onion and smoked fish or meat, eaten with fufu or rice.
ranking.history: The African eggplant is a vegetable native to West Africa whose leaves and fruit are both edible, nutritious and easy to grow, and a common crop in southern household gardens. "Gboma" is the Ewe name and "dessi" means sauce or stew, so the dish has a strong Ewe cultural flavor. It is very common on everyday household tables and is one of the most representative vegetable dishes of Togo.

ranking.name: Peanut stew
ranking.description: Peanuts are ground into a paste and simmered with chicken or lamb, tomato and chili into a thick sauce, rich in flavor, eaten with fufu, rice or maize porridge.
ranking.history: The peanut is native to South America; after the Portuguese brought it to West Africa in the 16th century it was widely grown in the dry northern savanna and became an important source of protein and fat. In northern Togo the Kabiye and Tem make peanut stew a daily main dish, and in the colonial period peanuts were also an export crop. This stew later spread throughout the country and belongs to the same culinary tradition as the peanut stews of other West African countries.
